juju · Phase 10 · AI agents

From a crash to a pull request, without copying anything across

Fixing a production crash used to mean opening juju, reading the stack trace, finding the release, checking out the right code, and pasting all of that into an AI agent. Now the agent asks juju itself. It reads the crash and the commit that crashed, and when it opens a fix, it records the pull request on the issue. juju never runs the agent and never sees your repository.

[phase 10] DONE verified="official MCP SDK client read issue 1 with commit 72925b4, linked a PR, resolved it; crash again → signed regression webhook accepted by an independent Python receiver; end-to-end test over the real queue and Postgres" tests="Go unit + integration, 81 dashboard"
The problem

A stack trace isn't enough to fix a bug

This is what an agent gets from juju's get_issue tool for a real crash sent to a local server during verification:

# Issue 1: TypeError: cart.items is undefined

Status: unresolved
Culprit: renderCart (src/cart.js)
Environments: production

## Releases (newest first)
- web@2.0.0: commit 72925b4bd9aa72b92b4d2bcc0deaae34d41021f1 in https://github.com/FrancisIje/juju

Stack trace, most recent call first (* = your code):
* renderCart  src/cart.js:42:17
  commitRoot  node_modules/react-dom/cjs/react-dom.js:100

Breadcrumbs, oldest first (what happened just before):
- [navigation] /checkout
- [http] GET /api/cart 500

Three things in it come from earlier phases: the readable frame (symbolication), the breadcrumbs (the SDKs), and grouping into one issue. The new line is the commit. Without it, the agent knows only "web@2.0.0" and reads today's code. If the bug is already half-fixed, or the file has moved, it fixes the wrong thing.

Try it

The loop, one step at a time

Each step shows what was really sent during the manual run against a local juju server.


    

  


  

    How it works
    
Four pieces, each for a reason


    

      
The commit is recorded on the server, not sent by the SDKs

      
CI runs juju release -name web@2.0.0 after the build. It reads the commit from git rev-parse HEAD and the repository from the origin remote, and stores them against the release name.

      
WhyEvery SDK already sends a release. Mapping release → commit on the server makes it work for web, React Native and Flutter apps with no SDK change and no app update. It also keeps the commit out of every event payload.

      
Why it strips the URLA CI checkout's remote often holds a token: https://x-access-token:ghs_…@github.com/acme/web. The CLI drops the user name and password, and the server refuses any URL that still has one. Otherwise the token would be stored and shown to everyone on the team.

    


    

      
MCP is served by juju itself

      
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is how coding agents call outside tools. juju answers it at POST /api/v1/projects/{id}/mcp with the project's secret key. Connecting an agent is one command:

      
claude mcp add --transport http juju https://myjuju.dev/api/v1/projects/1/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $JUJU_SECRET_KEY"

      

        
readlist_issues
Filter by status, text and environment; sort by recency or users affected.

        
readget_issue
The crash report above: frames, breadcrumbs, tags, context, commits, linked fixes.

        
readlist_issue_events
Recent raw events, to compare users, devices and inputs.

        
writelink_issue
Attach the pull request. The same URL again updates the title instead of adding a duplicate.

        
writeupdate_issue
Resolve, ignore or reopen.

      

      
Why on the server, not an installed programA program people install (a "stdio" MCP server) needs Node or Go on every laptop and CI runner, and an update on each. A URL needs nothing. The endpoint is stateless: no session, every request carries the key, so any juju process can answer it and a restart loses nothing.

      
Why mistakes come back as resultsA bad argument ("issue 999", "status: done") returns a normal result marked isError with a sentence saying what's wrong. The model reads it and tries again. A protocol error would only tell the client something broke.

      
Why it checks OriginAn agent doesn't send an Origin header; a browser always does. A request from any other site's page is refused, so a page that got hold of a key can't use someone's browser to call it.

      
The same actions are plain HTTP for scripts: GET …/issues/{id}, POST …/issues/{id}/status, POST …/issues/{id}/links, POST …/releases.

    


    

      
A signed webhook starts agents without a person

      
Next to Slack and email, an alert can go to any URL as JSON: the issue, its link, and the release's commit. Two headers come with it:

      
X-Juju-Timestamp: 1793008977
X-Juju-Signature: sha256=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of "1793008977." + body, keyed with the signing secret>

      
Why sign itThe receiver probably starts a paid agent run. Anyone who finds its URL could post a fake issue to it. Only juju and the receiver know the secret, so a matching signature proves where the call came from and that the body wasn't changed.

      
Why the timestamp is inside the signatureWithout it, someone who captured one real call could replay it forever. The receiver refuses calls older than a few minutes, and the timestamp can't be changed without breaking the signature.

      
Why the secret is shown onceLike the project secret key: the dashboard shows it in the response that created it, never on a reload. "New signing secret" replaces it.

    


    

      
The agent links; a person resolves

      
The example GitHub Actions workflow (examples/agent-fix) lets Claude Code read the issue, fix it on a branch, open a pull request and call link_issue. It doesn't give it update_issue.

      
WhyAn issue resolved before the fix ships would come straight back as a "regression" on the next crash, and the signal that a fix didn't work would be lost in noise. Resolving after the merge keeps regressions meaningful. The linked PR still shows on the issue page right away, so nobody starts a second fix.

    

  


  

    Using it
    
Set it up

    

      CI, after each release build
      
export JUJU_URL=https://myjuju.dev JUJU_PROJECT=1 JUJU_SECRET_KEY=sk_...
juju upload dist/                  # source maps, as before
juju release -name web@$VERSION    # new: which commit this release is

    

    

      Cursor and other MCP clients (.cursor/mcp.json)
      
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "juju": {
      "url": "https://myjuju.dev/api/v1/projects/1/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:JUJU_SECRET_KEY}" }
    }
  }
}

    

    

      Checking the webhook signature (Node)
      
const want = "sha256=" + crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${ts}.${rawBody}`).digest("hex");
const fresh = Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(ts)) < 300;
const ok = fresh && crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(sig), Buffer.from(want)); // lengths must match first

    

    
The dashboard has all of this ready to copy for each project under Settings → AI agents, with the project's own address filled in.

"-  [navigation] /checkout"
The first manual run showed a double space before each breadcrumb that had no timestamp. The tests had always given breadcrumbs timestamps. The timestamp is now left out when empty, and the integration test checks a breadcrumb without one.

      
"links its PR and resolves it"
The first version of the AI agents tab said the agent resolves the issue, while the workflow and README leave that to a person after the merge. The tab now says the same as the rest.

    

  


  

    Limits
    
Not covered yet

    
    
      
  • juju doesn't run agents itself. Someone has to run the workflow or a receiver. A juju-hosted agent would need repository access and a sandbox, which is a separate decision.
    • 
      
  • Starting a GitHub Action straight from the webhook needs a small relay: GitHub's repository_dispatch wants a GitHub token, which juju doesn't hold.
    • 
      
  • The secret key is all-or-nothing for a project: an agent that can read issues can also resolve them. Read-only keys would need key scopes.
    • 
      
  • The example workflow was checked as valid YAML but not run on GitHub, and connecting with the claude mcp add command was not tried (the official SDK client was).
    • 
      
  • Commit links use <repository>/commit/<sha>, which works for GitHub, GitLab and Gitea. Bitbucket uses /commits/ and opens a 404.
    • 
      
  • Webhooks share the limit of 30 alerts per project per hour with Slack and email.
    •
